## Why Am I Not Showing Up on Google Maps? (Contractor Fix List)
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/why-am-i-not-showing-up-on-google-maps/

**Short answer:** If you're invisible in the map pack, it's almost never bad luck. It's one of five fixable things: an incomplete profile, not enough reviews, the wrong service area, a name/address/phone mismatch, or a suspension you were never told about. Work the list in order.

### 1. Your profile isn't finished
*An incomplete profile can't outrank a complete one.*
Google ranks what it can verify. Every empty field — services, hours, service area, description, categories, photos — is a reason to rank someone else. Fill all of it, pick the most specific primary category you legitimately fit, and add job photos weekly. This is free, and it's the single highest-return hour in contractor marketing. Full list: the Google Business Profile checklist.

### 2. You don't have enough reviews yet
*Review count is the bar — and it's higher than most shops think.*
The shops sitting in the map pack aren't there on charm. The median HVAC shop ranking locally carries about 519 reviews; for plumbers it's about 337. If you have 20, you're not competing yet — you're warming up. And 91% of homeowners won't even consider a shop rated under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), so rating and volume both matter. Start here: how to get your first 50 reviews.

### 3. Your service area is wrong
*You rank near where you're based, not everywhere you drive.*
Contractors routinely set a 60-mile service radius and wonder why they rank nowhere. Proximity to the searcher is a real factor — a huge radius doesn't buy you reach, it just dilutes you. Set the areas you actually work, and build separate proof (reviews mentioning the town, job photos, a page per city) for the places you want to win.

### 4. Your name, address, and phone don't match everywhere
*Inconsistent NAP data makes you look like two businesses.*
If your shop is "Smith Heating & Air" on Google, "Smith HVAC" on Facebook, and an old cell number on three directories, Google has to guess which listing is real. Pick one exact name/address/phone and make every listing match it, character for character. This is boring and it works.

### 5. You're suspended — and nobody emailed you
*Suspended listings vanish with no warning.*
Suspensions happen over things like a virtual office address, keyword stuffing in the business name, or a category change. Sign in to your profile and look for a suspension notice. If you're suspended, no amount of posting fixes it — you appeal first, then rebuild.

### Then: don't waste the ranking you earn
*Ranking sends the call. Answering it books the job.*
Showing up is only half of it. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), replying in 5 minutes rather than 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026), and the average shop still misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026). Getting into the map pack and then missing the phone is the most expensive mistake in this whole list.

### FAQ
**Q: Why is my business not showing up on Google Maps?**
A: Usually one of five things: an incomplete Google Business Profile, too few reviews to compete (median ~519 for HVAC, ~337 for plumbers), a service area set too wide, inconsistent name/address/phone across listings, or a suspension you weren't notified about. Work them in that order.

**Q: How long does it take to rank in the Google map pack?**
A: Months, not days — and it tracks your review growth more than anything else. 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), so build rating and volume steadily rather than chasing a shortcut.

**Q: Does a bigger service area help me rank in more towns?**
A: No. Proximity matters, so an oversized radius dilutes you instead of extending you. Set the areas you actually serve and build real proof — reviews, photos, a page per city — for the towns you want to win.

---
## How to Respond to a Bad Review (Contractor Templates That Work)
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/how-to-respond-to-a-bad-review/

**Short answer:** The reply isn't for the person who left the review. It's for the hundred homeowners who'll read it while deciding whether to call you. Short, calm, specific, and offline — that's the whole formula, and it turns a 1-star into proof you're a pro.

### Write it for the next customer, not the angry one
*Your reply is public sales copy.*
You will almost never change the reviewer's mind. You will absolutely change what the next reader thinks. 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026) — but a calm, specific reply under a bad review reads as competence, and buyers notice. Treat every reply as a two-sentence ad for how you handle problems.

### The formula: acknowledge, correct the record, take it offline
*Three short moves, no argument.*
Acknowledge the frustration in one line. Add one factual detail that quietly corrects the record (the date, the scope, the warranty you offered). Then give a name and a number and move it off the platform. Three sentences. Never four paragraphs — length reads as guilt.

### Templates you can paste today
*Copy, swap the details, post within 24 hours.*
Wrong expectation: "Thanks for the feedback, Dana — I'm sorry the timeline felt long. Our quote covered the coil replacement only, and the parts shipped on the 14th. I'd still like to make this right: call me directly at 555-0147. — Mike, owner."Not our customer: "We take every review seriously, but we don't have a job on record at this address. If we worked with you under another name, please call me at 555-0147 so I can look into it. — Mike, owner."We genuinely blew it: "You're right, and I'm sorry. We missed the window and didn't call ahead. I've refunded the trip charge and we've changed how we confirm appointments. If you'll give us another shot, ask for me. — Mike, owner."

### What never to say
*No arguing, no legal threats, no customer details.*
Don't relitigate the invoice line by line. Don't mention lawyers. Don't post the customer's address, health details, or payment history. And don't ask for the review to be taken down in public — that reads as a shop that argues, which is exactly what the next homeowner is scanning for.

### The real fix is volume
*Bury a bad review under honest new ones.*
One 1-star out of 300 is a rounding error. One out of nine is your identity. The shops winning the map pack carry about 519 reviews (HVAC) and about 337 (plumbers) — at that volume a bad review costs you almost nothing. Build the habit: the one-tap review system and how to get more Google reviews.

### Never buy your way out of it
*Fake reviews are a bet against your own listing.*
Buying reviews risks the listing that your whole local presence sits on — and a suspended profile takes every real review with it. More on that trade: the fake-review risk.

### FAQ
**Q: Should I respond to every bad review?**
A: Yes, within about 24 hours, in three sentences: acknowledge, add one factual detail, and move it offline with a name and number. The reply is written for the next reader, not the reviewer.

**Q: Can I get a bad Google review removed?**
A: Only if it violates Google's policies (spam, off-topic, personal attacks, a competitor). You can flag it, but don't count on removal and never demand it publicly — respond calmly instead and out-volume it with real reviews.

**Q: How much does one bad review actually hurt?**
A: It depends entirely on volume. 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), so one 1-star against a handful of reviews is serious — against a few hundred it barely moves your rating.

---
## Is Nextdoor Worth It for Contractors? The Honest Answer
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/is-nextdoor-worth-it-for-contractors/

**Short answer:** Nextdoor's free side — neighbors recommending you by name — is one of the better lead sources a local shop can have, and it costs nothing. The paid side is a different product entirely. Judge it the same way you judge everything else: cost per booked job.

### The free side is the good side
*Neighbor recommendations are warm, exclusive, and free.*
When a neighbor asks "who do you use for plumbing?" and three people type your name, that's the warmest lead in local marketing: exclusive, pre-vouched, and zero cost per lead. Claim your business page, keep it accurate, and ask happy customers to recommend you there the same way you ask for a Google review.

### The paid side has to earn its place
*Judge it on cost per booked job, not impressions.*
Every channel gets the same test in this shop: what does a booked job cost? A booked job runs ~$542 via Angi versus ~$168 via Google Local Service Ads once close rates are counted. If Nextdoor ads land under your Google LSA number, keep spending. If they don't, that money belongs in LSA or reviews. That's the whole decision. Do the math: cost per booked job calculator.

### It won't replace Google — it stacks on it
*Nextdoor is a referral amplifier, not a search engine.*
People go to Nextdoor to ask their neighbors and to Google to find a pro right now. You need the second one working regardless: 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), and the map pack is still where the urgent, ready-to-book calls come from. Treat Nextdoor as extra referral surface, not a substitute.

### Answer Nextdoor leads like they're on fire
*Speed decides who gets the recommendation thread.*
Recommendation threads move in hours. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), and replying in 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026). A neighborhood thread you answer on Thursday for a Tuesday post is a thread someone else already won.

### How to test it in 60 days
*Small budget, tracked number, one honest decision.*
Run a small monthly budget, use a distinct tracking number or a "how'd you hear about us?" field, and count booked jobs, not leads. At 60 days, divide spend by jobs. Under your LSA cost — scale it. Over — kill it without sentiment. That's the same test that saves contractors from every shiny channel: evaluate any marketing with simple math.

### FAQ
**Q: Is Nextdoor worth it for contractors?**
A: The free business page and neighbor recommendations are worth the setup time for almost every local shop — exclusive, warm, no per-lead cost. Paid Nextdoor ads are only worth it if they book jobs for less than your best channel, which for most contractors is Google LSA at ~$168 per booked job vs ~$542 via Angi.

**Q: Are Nextdoor leads better than Angi leads?**
A: A neighbor recommendation is usually far better than a shared platform lead, because it's exclusive and comes with a vouch. Shared leads get sold to as many as 12 pros, which is why a booked job through Angi averages ~$542 vs ~$168 on Google LSA.

**Q: How do I get recommended on Nextdoor?**
A: Claim your page, keep hours and services accurate, and ask satisfied customers to recommend you there — the same habit that builds Google reviews. Then answer every thread fast; 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026).

---
## Email Marketing for Contractors: The Cheapest Repeat Work You Own
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/email-marketing-for-contractors/

**Short answer:** Every customer you've ever invoiced is a lead you already paid for. Email is the only channel where the list is yours, the cost is near zero, and nobody sells the same contact to eleven competitors. Four emails, sent on a schedule, out-earn most ad budgets.

### You already paid for this list
*Past customers are the cheapest jobs you'll ever book.*
You spent real money acquiring every name in your invoicing software — up to ~$542 per booked job on Angi, ~$168 on Google LSA. Emailing those people again costs effectively nothing. Most shops never do it, then buy new leads instead. That's paying full price twice.

### Own the list — don't rent the audience
*Social followers are borrowed. An email list is yours.*
An algorithm decides who sees your Facebook post. Nobody decides who sees your email but you. Build the list from every job: ask for the email on the invoice, on the estimate, at the door. Same logic as the profile and reviews you own — see referrals and repeat customers.

### The four emails that book jobs
*Seasonal reminder, maintenance due, review ask, and a last-year follow-up.*
1. Seasonal reminder — "It's April; let's check the system before the first 95° day." 2. Maintenance due — triggered off the last service date, the highest-booking email most shops never send. 3. Review ask — a few days after the job, one link, one sentence; that's how you close the gap on the ~519 reviews (HVAC) and ~337 (plumbers) the map-pack shops carry. 4. Last-year follow-up — "We were out a year ago for the water heater; anything need looking at?"

### How often, and what tone
*Monthly, useful, and written like a person.*
Once a month is plenty. Lead with something useful — what to check before the season turns, what a fair price looks like — and keep the sell to one line at the bottom. Homeowners forgive a plain email from a real contractor; they delete a newsletter that reads like a brochure.

### Answer the replies fast
*An email reply is a hot lead with a clock on it.*
When someone replies "yes, can you come look at it?", that's a booked job waiting on your response time. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), and 5 minutes versus 30 is up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026). Route the inbox to a phone somebody actually watches.

### FAQ
**Q: Does email marketing work for contractors?**
A: Yes, and it's the cheapest channel you own, because the list is made of customers you already paid to acquire — up to ~$542 per booked job via Angi, ~$168 via Google LSA. Re-reaching them costs nothing per send.

**Q: How often should a contractor email past customers?**
A: About once a month, plus triggered emails (maintenance due, seasonal reminder, post-job review ask). Useful first, one line of selling at the bottom.

**Q: What should I send in a contractor newsletter?**
A: Four repeatable emails cover most of the value: a seasonal reminder, a maintenance-due notice off the last service date, a post-job review ask, and a one-year follow-up. Plain text from the owner beats a designed brochure.

---
## Why Customers Ghost After an Estimate (And How to Get Them Back)
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/why-customers-ghost-after-an-estimate/

**Short answer:** You quoted it, they said "let me think about it," and then nothing. It's usually not the price — it's that someone else got there first, the quote was hard to say yes to, or nobody followed up. All three are fixable this week.

### Someone beat you to it
*Most ghosting happened before you ever quoted.*
78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026). If you got there third, you weren't in a price competition — you were the backup quote they collected to feel responsible. Replying in 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026). More: why 5 minutes matters.

### The quote was hard to say yes to
*One number and no next step invites delay.*
A bare total makes a homeowner do the work of deciding. Give them scope in plain language, what's included and excluded, two options where you can (good / better), and an explicit next step with a date: "Reply yes and I'll hold Thursday the 12th." Saying yes should take one sentence.

### They never trusted you enough to spend that much
*Proof closes the gap price can't.*
Big-ticket work needs proof attached to it: recent reviews, photos of the same job, license and insurance. 91% of homeowners won't even consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026) — that filtering doesn't stop once they've met you. Put the proof in the estimate, not just on the website.

### Nobody followed up
*Two touches recover jobs you already earned.*
Most shops quote and wait. Send a short message at 48 hours ("any questions on the scope?") and one at day 10 ("holding a slot next week if you still want it"). No pressure, no discount — just presence. This is free money: you already paid to get the lead and did the site visit.

### And check that you didn't miss the callback
*The average shop misses 14% of its calls.*
Sometimes they didn't ghost you — they called back and got voicemail. The average shop misses 14% of calls (CallRail 2026). Before you blame the price, look at the call log: missed calls cost invoices.

### FAQ
**Q: Why do customers ghost after getting an estimate?**
A: Usually not price. Most often someone responded faster (78% hire the first responder — Lead Connect 2026), the quote had no clear next step, there wasn't enough proof to trust a big spend, or nobody followed up. Missed callbacks account for more than owners think — the average shop misses 14% of calls (CallRail 2026).

**Q: How many times should I follow up on a quote?**
A: Twice is the sweet spot: a short check-in at about 48 hours and one at around day 10 offering a specific slot. No discounting, no pressure — just a clear, easy yes.

**Q: Should I lower my price if they go quiet?**
A: No. Discounting to chase silence trains customers to wait you out and eats the margin on the job. Fix speed, clarity, and proof first — those recover more quotes than a price cut.

## The Contractor Marketing Calendar: What to Do Every Month
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/contractor-marketing-calendar/

**Short answer:** Marketing fails for contractors because it's done in panic bursts when the schedule goes quiet. This is the boring version that works: a weekly habit, a monthly habit, and one seasonal push — all of it under three hours a month.

### The weekly 20 minutes
*Reviews, photos, and every unanswered lead.*
Ask this week's customers for a review, post two job photos to your Google Business Profile, and clear every unreturned call and message. That's it. Reviews are the compounding asset — the shops in the map pack carry about 519 (HVAC) and 337 (plumbers) — and 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026).

### The monthly hour
*Check the numbers, email the list, fix one page.*
Add up spend and jobs booked per channel and kill whatever costs more than your best channel (Google LSA runs ~$168 per booked job vs ~$542 on Angi). Send one email to past customers. Fix one thing on your site — around 98% of contractor-website visitors leave without contacting anyone (WebFX 2026), and it's usually the phone number, the load time, or the missing proof.

### Spring: capacity season
*Demand comes to you — protect the phone.*
March through June you don't need more leads, you need to not lose the ones arriving. The average shop misses 14% of calls (CallRail 2026) and 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026). Staff the phone, shorten quote turnaround, and bank reviews while volume is high — you'll live off them in January.

### Summer and fall: harvest and pre-book
*Turn peak volume into next season's schedule.*
Peak season is when your review count should climb fastest — every completed job is an ask. Fall is for pre-booking: email past customers about seasonal service before the first cold snap, and get maintenance work on the calendar while they're thinking about it.

### Winter: the slow-month plan
*Work the list you already own.*
Slow months are for the free channels: past-customer emails, referral asks, finishing the Google profile, and building the pages you never had time to write. Don't panic-buy shared leads in January — that's exactly when the ~$542-per-booked-job math hurts most. See surviving the slow season.

### Do this before you add anything
*The order matters more than the effort.*
Owned channels first (profile, reviews, past customers), then speed to lead, then your website, then paid. Adding an ad budget on top of a broken phone process is how contractors conclude "marketing doesn't work." The full order of operations: start here.

### FAQ
**Q: How much time should a contractor spend on marketing each month?**
A: About three hours, spent on the same things every month: 20 minutes weekly on reviews, job photos, and unanswered leads, plus one monthly hour to check cost per booked job, email past customers, and fix one thing on your website.

**Q: What should contractors do in the slow season?**
A: Work the channels you already own — past-customer emails, referral asks, completing your Google Business Profile, and writing the pages you never had time for. Panic-buying shared leads in a slow month is where the ~$542-per-booked-job math hurts most vs ~$168 on Google LSA.

**Q: When should I ask for reviews?**
A: Every week, at the end of every completed job, while it's fresh. Volume is the whole game — map-pack shops carry roughly 519 reviews (HVAC) and 337 (plumbers), and 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026).

## Missed Call Text Back: The Cheapest Fix in Contractor Marketing
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/missed-call-text-back-for-contractors/

**Short answer:** The average shop misses 14% of its calls, and a homeowner with a leak does not leave a voicemail — they dial the next number. An automatic text sent the second you miss the call puts you back in the conversation before your competitor picks up. It costs a few dollars a month and recovers jobs you already paid to generate.

### You already paid for the call you just missed
*A missed call is a lead you bought and threw away.*
Every ringing phone cost something to create — an ad, a review, a profile, a referral you earned. A booked job runs ~$542 through Angi versus ~$168 through Google Local Service Ads, and the average shop still misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026). That's not a phone problem, it's a budget problem: you're paying full price for leads and dropping one in seven on the floor. More on the size of it: what missed calls actually cost.

### Homeowners don't leave voicemails anymore
*They hang up and dial the next contractor.*
Someone standing in two inches of water is not composing a message. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), which means the winner of that job is usually decided in the next four minutes, without you. Voicemail is a system designed for a customer who no longer exists.

### What missed call text back actually is
*An automatic text fires the instant a call goes unanswered.*
It's a setting, not a project. When a call rings out, your phone system sends the caller a text immediately — before they've finished dialing the next shop. Most VoIP providers, answering services, and contractor CRMs include it; standalone versions run a few dollars a month. If you do one thing to your marketing this month, do this one.

### What the text should say
*Name the shop, apologize once, ask one question.*
Three lines, no marketing voice: "This is Mike at Smith Heating & Air — sorry we missed you, we're on a job. What's going on and what's your address? I'll get you on the schedule." Naming the business stops it reading as spam, the apology buys ten seconds of patience, and one question gets them typing instead of dialing. Don't send a link. Don't send a form. Ask a question a person answers with their thumbs.

### Speed is the whole product
*Instant beats good; five minutes beats thirty.*
The text has to fire in seconds, not after a five-minute delay someone helpfully configured. Replying in 5 minutes rather than 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026), and an automatic text is the only way to hit that number while you're under a house. Then answer the reply like it's on fire — see why five minutes matters.

### Fix the phone before you raise the budget
*Ad spend on a broken phone is just faster waste.*
Doubling your ad budget while missing 14% of calls buys you more missed calls. The order of operations never changes: answer the phone, then earn reviews, then fix the website, then spend. 98% of contractor-website visitors leave without calling (WebFX 2026) — the few who do call are the entire return on everything else you're paying for. Run your own number: the missed call revenue calculator.

### FAQ
**Q: What is missed call text back?**
A: An automatic text message sent to a caller the moment their call goes unanswered, usually built into your VoIP system or contractor CRM. It puts you back in the conversation within seconds, which matters because 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026).

**Q: Do missed call text backs actually work for contractors?**
A: They recover leads you already paid to generate. The average shop misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026), homeowners with an urgent problem rarely leave voicemails, and replying in 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026).

**Q: What should a missed call auto-text say?**
A: Name your business, apologize in one line, and ask one question: what's going on and what's the address. Keep it under three lines, skip links and forms, and make sure it fires in seconds rather than minutes.

## Service Area Pages: How to Rank in the Towns You Drive To
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/service-area-pages-for-contractors/

**Short answer:** You rank near where you sit, not everywhere you drive. Setting a 60-mile radius on your Google profile doesn't extend you — it dilutes you. What actually wins the next town over is a real page about real work you did there, backed by reviews that say the town's name.

### Proximity is real, and a wide radius doesn't beat it
*You rank near your address, not across your whole service area.*
The most common contractor mistake in local SEO is setting the service radius to everywhere the truck can reach and waiting. Distance from the searcher is a genuine ranking factor, so a 60-mile radius doesn't buy reach — it just spreads thin proof across a lot of towns. If you're invisible in your own town first, start here instead: why you're not showing up on Google Maps.

### What a real service area page looks like
*One town, real jobs, real photos, real names.*
A page that ranks for "plumber in Willis" talks about Willis: the neighborhoods you work, the jobs you've done there, photos from those jobs, the response time from your shop, and reviews from customers in that town. It reads like a contractor wrote it about a place they actually go. Two hundred words of that beat two thousand words of filler.

### The doorway-page trap
*Fifty copies with the city swapped is a penalty waiting to happen.*
The templated approach — one page duplicated across every town in the county with find-and-replace on the city name — is the thing search engines have spent twenty years learning to ignore. It doesn't just fail to rank; a pile of thin near-duplicate pages drags on the site that hosts it. Build three towns properly instead of thirty badly.

### Reviews are how you actually claim a town
*A review that names the town is a ranking signal and a sales asset.*
Nothing tells a search engine you work in a place like customers from that place saying so. Map-pack shops carry roughly 519 reviews (HVAC) and 337 (plumbers), and 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026). When you finish a job out of town, ask for that review the same day and let the customer mention where they live naturally. Systemize it: the one-tap review system.

### Build them in order of profit, not alphabetically
*Start with the towns you'd actually drive to for a good job.*
Rank the towns by what a job there is worth after the drive. Build the top three pages, earn reviews there, and only then add the fourth. A service area page for a town you'd resent driving to is a page you'll never support with real jobs or real proof — and unsupported pages don't rank.

### Then answer the phone the page earns
*Out-of-town leads are the easiest ones to lose.*
A homeowner two towns over is calling three shops, not one. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), 5 minutes beats 30 by up to 100x (MIT Sloan 2026), and the average shop misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026). Ranking in a new town and missing its calls is the most expensive way to do local SEO.

### FAQ
**Q: Do service area pages actually work for contractors?**
A: Real ones do. A page about one town — with jobs you did there, photos, and reviews from local customers — can rank. Fifty templated copies with the city name swapped generally don't, and a pile of thin near-duplicate pages can hold back the rest of your site.

**Q: How do I rank in a town I'm not located in?**
A: Build genuine proof for it: a substantive page about your work in that town, job photos, and reviews from customers who live there. Proximity to the searcher is a real ranking factor, so you're overcoming distance with evidence — which is why review volume matters (map-pack shops carry roughly 519 reviews for HVAC, 337 for plumbers).

**Q: Should I set a big service area radius on my Google Business Profile?**
A: No. Set the areas you genuinely work. An oversized radius doesn't extend your reach, it spreads thin proof across many towns — and you still rank primarily near where you're based.

## How Much Should a Contractor Website Cost? (Honest Ranges)
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/how-much-should-a-contractor-website-cost/

**Short answer:** There's no right price, only a right test: does the site book jobs for less than your other channels? Most contractors overpay for design and underpay for the four things that actually convert. Here's what's worth money, what isn't, and how to know within ninety days.

### Price the site the way you price everything else
*Cost per booked job, not cost per page.*
A website isn't a purchase, it's a channel — and every channel in this shop gets the same test: what does a booked job cost? A booked job runs ~$542 through Angi and ~$168 through Google Local Service Ads. If your site pays for itself in booked work inside a year, the price was right. If it doesn't, no amount of beautiful was worth it. Run it: cost per booked job calculator.

### What you're actually buying
*Four things convert; the rest is decoration.*
A phone number visible without scrolling. Proof on the first screen — reviews, real job photos, the trades you actually do. A page that loads fast on a phone in a truck. And a form that reaches somebody in minutes. 98% of contractor-website visitors leave without calling (WebFX 2026); those four items are the whole fight for the other 2%. The longer version: why your site isn't converting.

### What's worth paying for
*Speed, mobile, proof, and someone who'll change it next year.*
Pay for a site that loads fast, works one-handed on a phone, puts your proof up front, and can be edited without an invoice every time your hours change. Pay for real photos of your own trucks and crews. That's a real budget, and it's usually a lot less than what gets quoted.

### What's pure markup
*Custom animation, stock photos, and monthly fees for nothing.*
Sliders, parallax, and a video header don't book jobs — they slow down the phone in the truck. Neither do stock photos of models in clean hard hats; homeowners can spot them, and they undercut the proof you're paying to build. Watch for a monthly "maintenance" fee attached to a site nobody touches, and for the hosting markup game: what the markup looks like.

### Own the site, whoever builds it
*Your domain, your hosting, your logins — always.*
The single most expensive mistake isn't the build price, it's discovering the agency owns your domain, your hosting, and your Google profile. Get admin access to everything in writing before the first payment. If that's a problem for them, it's the answer: when an agency won't share access.

### The 90-day test
*Count booked jobs, then decide.*
Put a tracking number on it, ask every caller how they found you, and at ninety days divide what you spent by the jobs it booked. Under your best channel — keep going. Over — the problem is the site, not the budget. And make sure it isn't the phone: the average shop misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026), which makes a perfectly good website look like a bad one.

### FAQ
**Q: How much should a contractor website cost?**
A: There's no universal number — judge it on cost per booked job like any other channel. A booked job runs about $542 via Angi and about $168 via Google Local Service Ads; if the site books work under that inside a year, it was priced right.

**Q: What makes a contractor website actually convert?**
A: Four things: a phone number visible without scrolling, proof (reviews and real job photos) on the first screen, fast loading on a phone, and a form that reaches a human in minutes. 98% of visitors leave without calling (WebFX 2026), so everything else is decoration.

**Q: Should I pay a monthly fee for my contractor website?**
A: Only for something you actually receive — hosting, real edits, real reporting. Be sure you own the domain, the hosting account, and every login before you pay anything; agencies holding those hostage is the most expensive website problem there is.

## Do Contractors Need a CRM? The Honest Answer
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/crm-for-contractors-do-you-need-one/

**Short answer:** Most contractors don't lose jobs because they lack software. They lose them because a lead sat unanswered for four hours and an estimate never got followed up. A CRM is worth paying for the day it fixes those two things — and not one day sooner.

### The real question isn't features, it's leaks
*Buy software to plug a specific leak you can name.*
Every CRM demo shows you scheduling, dispatch, invoicing, and a dashboard. None of that is why a shop's revenue is short. The leaks are almost always the same two: leads that sat too long, and estimates nobody chased. If a tool fixes those, it's cheap at almost any price. If it doesn't, it's a monthly fee for a prettier version of the problem.

### Leak one: response time
*Speed is the single highest-value thing to automate.*
78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), and replying in 5 minutes rather than 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026). Meanwhile the average shop misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026). The first thing any CRM has to do is get a text or a call back out in minutes without a human remembering — see missed call text back.

### Leak two: the estimate nobody followed up
*Most quotes die of silence, not price.*
Sent quotes are the warmest pipeline a contractor has and the most neglected. A tool that automatically nudges every open estimate at day two and day seven pays for itself in one job, because it's chasing work you already did the site visit for. Why they go quiet: why customers ghost after an estimate.

### When a spreadsheet is genuinely enough
*One truck, one phone, and a habit that holds.*
If you're a one-truck shop and you personally answer every call, a shared sheet with name, job, date quoted, and next-touch date works fine. The system that matters is the habit, not the software. Software becomes necessary when leads arrive faster than one person can hold in their head — usually the second truck, or the first office hire.

### It also owns the cheapest list you have
*Past customers are jobs you already paid for.*
A CRM's quietest value is remembering every customer you've invoiced, so you can email them a year later. You paid up to ~$542 per booked job through Angi (~$168 via Google LSA) to acquire those names — re-reaching them costs nothing. See email marketing for contractors.

### How to buy one without regret
*Name the two numbers you expect it to move first.*
Before the trial, write down your current response time and your estimate follow-up rate. Trial one tool for thirty days and check both. If neither moved, the tool didn't fail — the process did, and a second tool won't fix it. Same test as every other line in the budget: evaluate any marketing with simple math.

### FAQ
**Q: Do contractors really need a CRM?**
A: Only if it plugs a leak you can name — usually slow lead response or un-chased estimates. A one-truck shop where the owner answers every call can run on a spreadsheet; the need shows up when leads arrive faster than one person can track.

**Q: What should a contractor CRM actually do?**
A: Get a reply out in minutes (78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first, Lead Connect 2026), automatically follow up open estimates, and keep every past customer reachable. Scheduling and invoicing are conveniences; those three are the revenue.

**Q: Is a spreadsheet enough instead of a CRM?**
A: For a single-truck shop, often yes — name, job, date quoted, and next-touch date will hold the pipeline if the habit holds. The habit is the system; the software just makes it survive a second truck.

## Water Damage Restoration Marketing: Winning the 2 A.M. Call
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/water-damage-restoration-marketing/

**Short answer:** Restoration is the most speed-sensitive trade there is. Nobody shops around at 2 a.m. with water coming through the ceiling — they call the first company that shows up in the map pack and answers on the first ring. Everything in restoration marketing is downstream of those two facts.

### Emergency demand rewards presence, not persuasion
*You win by being there and answering, not by convincing.*
A homeowner watching a ceiling come down isn't reading your About page. They search, they tap the first credible listing, and they call. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), and 5 minutes versus 30 is up to 100x more likely to connect (MIT Sloan 2026). For restoration that gap is measured in minutes, and the average shop still misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026). A missed 2 a.m. call is a whole job.

### 24/7 has to be real
*If the phone rolls to voicemail overnight, you don't do emergencies.*
Advertising emergency service and answering it are two different businesses. Whatever you can afford — a rotating on-call phone, an answering service, an auto-text the second a call is missed — the requirement is that a human replies in minutes at any hour. Start with the cheap version: missed call text back.

### The map pack is the whole storefront
*Urgent searches end in the map pack, not on page one.*
Complete every field on your Google Business Profile, set genuine 24-hour availability, and post job photos weekly. Then grind reviews: 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), and the shops holding local rankings carry serious volume — roughly 519 reviews for HVAC and 337 for plumbers is the neighborhood you're competing in. Checklist: the GBP checklist.

### Reviews carry more weight here than anywhere
*You're asking to be let into a house on the worst day of someone's year.*
Restoration asks for enormous trust under time pressure — strangers, insurance, and a wrecked home. Reviews that mention responsiveness and how the crew treated the house do more selling than any ad. Ask at the end of every job, while the relief is fresh: the one-tap review system.

### Referral relationships are the moat
*Plumbers, property managers, and adjusters send the steady work.*
Emergency search brings volume; relationships bring reliability. The plumber who stops the leak, the property manager with forty units, and the agent who fields the first call all need someone to hand the job to. Be reachable, show up fast, and never make them look bad — that's the entire pitch. More: referrals and repeat customers.

### Judge every paid channel the same way
*Cost per booked job, or it doesn't stay in the budget.*
Restoration leads get sold aggressively, and urgency makes bad channels look reasonable. Hold the line: a booked job runs ~$542 through Angi versus ~$168 through Google Local Service Ads. Anything you buy has to beat your best number on booked jobs, not leads. Do the math: cost per booked job calculator.

### FAQ
**Q: How do water damage restoration companies get leads?**
A: Mostly from urgent local search — the Google map pack — plus referral relationships with plumbers, property managers, and insurance contacts. Both reward the same thing: being reachable instantly, since 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026).

**Q: What's the most important marketing for a restoration company?**
A: Answering the phone 24/7 and holding a strong Google Business Profile with real review volume. 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), and the average business misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026) — in emergency work each miss is an entire job.

**Q: Are paid restoration leads worth it?**
A: Only if they beat your best channel on cost per booked job. A booked job averages about $542 via Angi versus about $168 via Google Local Service Ads — urgency is not a reason to skip that comparison.

## Remodeling Contractor Marketing: Selling a Long, Expensive Yes
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/remodeling-contractor-marketing/

**Short answer:** Remodeling isn't an emergency trade. Nobody calls three companies at midnight — they research for months, collect bids, and pick the contractor they trust with their house and their savings. That changes what marketing has to do: build proof over time, then survive the long gap between estimate and yes.

### The buying window is months, not minutes
*You're being evaluated long before the first call.*
A homeowner planning a kitchen looks at photos for months before anyone dials. That means your marketing's job isn't to catch a moment of urgency — it's to be findable and convincing during a long, quiet comparison. Portfolio depth, review volume, and a site that survives scrutiny do that work while you're on a job site.

### Photos are the product
*Before-and-after is the only portfolio that sells remodeling.*
Nobody buys a remodel from a description. Shoot every project — before, during, after — in decent light, and organize by room type so a bathroom buyer sees bathrooms. This is also the cheapest content you'll ever produce: the same photos feed your Google profile, your site, and your social. 98% of contractor-website visitors leave without calling (WebFX 2026), and thin proof is a big reason why.

### Reviews decide who makes the shortlist
*Big tickets mean buyers screen hard before they call.*
The bigger the check, the more homework. 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026) — on a five-figure remodel that filter is brutal, and reviews describing communication, schedule, and cleanliness matter more than any single job photo. Build volume steadily: your first 50 reviews.

### The estimate is where remodelers lose money
*Long decisions need follow-up, not hope.*
You spend hours on a design and a bid, then wait. Most quotes die of silence rather than price — and a remodeler's follow-up gap is measured in weeks, not days. Schedule the nudge before you leave the driveway. The playbook: why customers ghost after an estimate.

### Still answer fast — the first call is a screen
*Slow response reads as "they'll be slow on my job."*
Long consideration doesn't mean patient. 78% of homeowners hire whoever responds first (Lead Connect 2026), and on a remodel your response time is being read as a preview of how the project will run. The average shop misses 14% of its calls (CallRail 2026); on a $40,000 kitchen that's not a missed call, it's a missed year.

### Referrals are worth more than any ad here
*One finished kitchen sells the next three.*
Neighbors watch the dumpster and the trucks for six weeks. Ask for the review, ask for the referral, and leave the site cleaner than the neighbors expect. Compare that to buying it: a booked job runs ~$542 through Angi versus ~$168 through Google Local Service Ads — and neither one comes pre-vouched by someone the buyer knows.

### FAQ
**Q: How do remodeling contractors get more leads?**
A: Mostly through proof accumulated over a long consideration window: a deep before-and-after portfolio, strong review volume, and referrals from finished projects. 91% of homeowners won't consider a shop under 4 stars (BrightLocal 2026), which decides who even makes the shortlist.

**Q: What marketing works best for kitchen and bath remodelers?**
A: Photography and reviews, organized so a buyer sees projects like theirs. Then disciplined estimate follow-up — remodeling quotes usually die of silence during a weeks-long decision, not of price.

**Q: Should remodelers buy leads?**
A: Only against the same test as any trade: cost per booked job, not per lead. A booked job averages about $542 via Angi versus about $168 via Google Local Service Ads — and on long-consideration, high-ticket work, referrals and reviews usually out-earn both.

## AI Receptionist vs Missed-Call Text-Back: Do the Math
URL: https://booked-job.com/blog/ai-receptionist-or-missed-call-text-back/

**Short answer:** A $300/month AI receptionist vs a ~$30/month text-back. For most shops the cheap fix wins. Here's why.

### 
*An AI receptionist costs about ten times what a missed-call text-back does, and for most small shops it doesn't win you more jobs.*
You missed a call while you were under a sink. A salesperson has a pitch: an AI receptionist that answers every call, 24/7, in a friendly voice. It runs about $300 a month. That's $3,600 a year. Before you sign anything, do the arithmetic.The cheap alternative is missed-call text-back. A missed call fires an automatic text to the caller: "Sorry we missed you, this is Dave at Dave's Plumbing, what do you need?" That's often about $30 a month. Same job of not dropping the lead. One-tenth the price. The question isn't which is fancier. It's which one actually books the job.

### What a lead actually wants: a fast answer
*Leads go to whoever responds first, and a text in seconds beats a bot that fumbles a conversation.*
Here's the number that should drive every decision you make about your phone: responding in 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect with a lead, and 21x more likely to qualify it (Lead Response Management study, Prof. James Oldroyd). Speed is the whole game. A homeowner with a burst pipe calls three plumbers. The first human to call back usually wins.A missed-call text-back hits that window instantly. The caller gets a real text with your name, and they can just reply. You see it and call back. We walk through the setup in missed-call text-back for contractors and why speed to lead beats almost everything else you could spend money on.

### Where the $300 bot earns its keep (and where it doesn't)
*An AI receptionist only pays off at high call volume you genuinely can't staff — most small shops aren't there.*
Be fair to the expensive option. If you're a multi-truck shop drowning in calls and you're already losing real jobs to voicemail at noon, a receptionist that answers and books can pencil out. At enough volume, $3,600 a year is cheap next to the jobs you'd otherwise lose.But most shops aren't there. If you miss a handful of calls a day, you don't need a machine holding full conversations with your customers. You need the caller to know you saw them and to get a callback fast. The bot adds cost, a new failure point, and a layer between you and the person about to hand you money. Read our full take in is an AI receptionist worth it.

### The verdict for most shops
*Start with the ~$30 text-back; only reach for a receptionist when call volume proves you need it.*
Here's the honest call: for most one-to-three-truck shops, spend the $30, not the $300. Get missed-call text-back running this week. It closes the gap that's actually costing you jobs — the silent dropped call — without putting a robot in front of your customers.Revisit the AI receptionist only when your own call logs prove you're losing jobs you can't catch any other way. If you want a human to look at your numbers and tell you straight, talk to a person. And if you're shopping anyway, we compare the options in the best AI receptionist for contractors roundup.

### FAQ
**Q: How much does an AI receptionist cost for a contractor?**
A: A typical AI receptionist runs about $300 a month, which is roughly $3,600 a year. Missed-call text-back does the core job of not dropping a lead for about $30 a month. For most small shops the cheaper tool wins.

**Q: Does missed-call text-back actually work?**
A: Yes, because it hits the lead fast. Responding in 5 minutes instead of 30 makes you up to 100x more likely to connect with a lead (Lead Response Management study, Prof. James Oldroyd). A text that goes out the second you miss a call keeps you in that window.

**Q: When is an AI receptionist actually worth it?**
A: When you have enough call volume that you're losing real jobs to voicemail and can't staff a human to answer. At that point $3,600 a year can pencil out. Below that, you're paying for a robot you don't need.
